metadata.summary: Use rifaximin 550 mg twice daily for adult overt HE recurrence prevention. Preserve the lactulose evidence, distinguish acute guidance and correct triggers while monitoring function and safety.
metadata.application: Confirm the HE history and severity, correct triggers, titrate lactulose safely, select the indication-specific rifaximin regimen and arrange accessible treatment and liver follow-up.
keyPoints: The US HE regimen is 550 mg twice daily.
Combination evidence supports retaining tolerated lactulose.
Acute add-on guidance is distinct from the labeled indication.
Follow clinical recurrence and function, not ammonia alone.
Review severe hepatic exposure, interactions and medication access.

bodies.heading: Use the labeled outcome
bodies.body: Rifaximin acts mainly in the intestine and reduces gut bacterial contributions to ammonia production. The US indication is reduction in risk of overt hepatic encephalopathy recurrence in adults, using 550 mg orally twice daily with or without food. This is 1,100 mg daily; one 550 mg tablet per dose requires 60 tablets for a prescribed 30-day supply. The HE label does not specify a fixed 3-day or 14-day course. Duration and reassessment belong to the liver-care plan. The regimen does not diagnose HE, cure the underlying liver disease or provide systemic infection treatment.

bodies.heading: Read the placebo-controlled evidence in context
bodies.body: The pivotal six-month, double-blind trial enrolled 299 adults in remission after at least two HE episodes in the previous six months. Ninety-one percent received concomitant lactulose. Breakthrough HE occurred in 31/140 rifaximin recipients (22%) and 73/159 placebo recipients (46%); the label reports a 58% reduction from its time-to-event comparison, not a 58-percentage-point absolute reduction. HE-related hospitalization occurred in 19/140 (14%) versus 36/159 (23%), with a reported 50% time-to-event risk reduction. The small group not using lactulose could not establish a separate treatment effect. No participants had MELD scores above 25, and severe-liver-disease subgroup estimates were limited. Preserve these population and endpoint limits when discussing benefit.

bodies.heading: Preserve the lactulose partnership
bodies.body: The current label also reports a six-month, randomized, open-label trial of 222 adults with at least one recent overt HE episode. Breakthrough HE occurred in 28/113 patients taking rifaximin alone (25%) and 15/109 taking rifaximin plus lactulose (14%). The hazard ratio for monotherapy versus combination was 1.98 (95% CI 1.06 to 3.7), indicating greater breakthrough hazard with monotherapy in that trial. This is not a 98-percentage-point difference or proof that no patient can use rifaximin alone. Current ACG guidance favors the combination when tolerated and recommends adding rifaximin for recurrent episodes despite lactulose maintenance. Do not automatically withdraw effective lactulose when rifaximin begins; significant intolerance requires an individualized plan.

bodies.heading: Titrate the bowel plan safely
bodies.body: Lactulose is first-line outpatient prevention after an initial overt episode. Aim for about 2 to 3 soft stools daily, considering stool consistency as well as frequency. Excess catharsis can cause dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities that precipitate further HE. If there are frequent watery stools, weakness or poor intake, reassess lactulose dosing, hydration, electrolytes and cognition rather than increasing the dose or assuming rifaximin prevents these harms. Confirm adherence, tolerance and medication access before labeling a recurrence as failure of an adequate regimen.

bodies.heading: Separate acute guidance from the label
bodies.body: The 2026 ACG guideline conditionally suggests rifaximin added to lactulose for acute overt HE, with low-certainty evidence. This is distinct from the US labeled recurrence-prevention indication. The book lists an older off-label 400 mg every-8-hour, 5-to-10-day acute regimen; do not substitute that schedule for labeled 550 mg twice-daily prevention or present it as the only current acute pathway. Rifaximin initiation does not replace clinical diagnosis, stabilization, lactulose when appropriate or treatment of a precipitant. An obtunded patient needs urgent airway and route assessment before oral medication.

bodies.heading: Correct the precipitant and evaluate mimics
bodies.body: Evaluate new confusion clinically, using the time course, baseline cognition, examination and caregiver history. Assess glucose, infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, constipation, dehydration or excessive diuresis, kidney dysfunction, electrolyte disturbances, sedating drugs and missed therapy. Infection and HE can coexist; hospitalized ascites with suspected infection warrants diagnostic paracentesis. New focal neurological deficits, seizures or head trauma require urgent neurological evaluation and indicated imaging. Rifaximin is not adequate treatment for bacteremia, sepsis or SBP; those conditions require their own diagnostic and antimicrobial care alongside the HE plan.

bodies.heading: Monitor the patient, not a drug level
bodies.body: Track mental status, daily function, falls, recurrent overt episodes, HE-related admissions, bowel quality, hydration, electrolytes, adherence and liver trajectory. Rifaximin concentrations are not the routine outcome used to judge HE prevention. An elevated ammonia concentration alone does not establish the diagnosis or justify dose escalation. If an obtained ammonia value is normal, reconsider other causes of confusion in addition to HE; do not automatically exclude HE solely from that result. The clinical examination and response to precipitant treatment guide reassessment.

bodies.heading: Recognize increased exposure and interactions
bodies.body: Minimal usual absorption does not eliminate risk in advanced liver disease. The US label describes approximately 10-, 14- and 21-fold higher systemic exposure in Child-Pugh A, B and C patients, respectively, than in healthy volunteers. It recommends no routine hepatic dose adjustment because of local action, but requires caution in severe Child-Pugh C impairment. Cyclosporine and other P-glycoprotein inhibitors can further increase exposure. Review the need for the combination and monitor appropriately rather than calling severe impairment an absolute contraindication or assuming interaction risk is absent. With concomitant warfarin, monitor INR and prothrombin time and adjust warfarin when needed.

bodies.heading: Keep serious adverse effects visible
bodies.body: Rifaximin is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to rifaximin, rifamycin antibiotics or product components. Peripheral edema, nausea, dizziness, fatigue and ascites appear in HE safety data; a new symptom still requires clinical assessment rather than automatic attribution to the drug or liver disease. C. difficile-associated diarrhea remains possible during or after antibiotic therapy, so persistent or worsening diarrhea is not always lactulose excess. Stop rifaximin and obtain urgent clinical evaluation for severe hypersensitivity or signs of a severe skin reaction. The current label reports SJS/TEN in cirrhosis and rhabdomyolysis with or without concomitant statins; muscle symptoms require evaluation.

bodies.heading: Protect nutrition and muscle
bodies.body: Do not routinely restrict protein to treat HE. Muscle loss reduces an important route of ammonia handling and contributes to frailty. Current ACG guidance recommends 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein in outpatients with HE, with an individualized nutrition plan and adequate intake; a late-night snack may help. Vegetable or dairy protein can support tolerance without becoming a reason to underfeed. BCAA supplementation can be considered when food alone cannot meet protein needs. Zinc is an adjunct for documented low zinc with persistent symptoms despite lactulose and rifaximin, not a universal substitute for either medicine.

bodies.heading: Reassess persistent disease and procedure-related risk
bodies.body: If mental status does not recover after 48 to 72 hours of adequate therapy and precipitant reversal, reassess missed infection, drugs, metabolic or neurological disease and portosystemic shunts. Deterioration requires immediate care rather than waiting for that interval. Refractory HE may warrant specialist shunt assessment. Separately, ACG 2026 recommends starting rifaximin 14 days before elective TIPS and continuing for at least six months in decompensated cirrhosis, with or without previous overt HE. This is procedure-specific guidance beyond the labeled recurrence indication; it is not a reason to delay an emergency procedure.

bodies.heading: Make prevention executable
bodies.body: Assign a clinician to follow recurrence, tolerance and liver progression. Provide patients and caregivers a written bowel plan, reliable medication supply and instructions for worsening confusion, bleeding, fever, profuse diarrhea or inability to take medicines. Address affordability and refill interruptions before discharge. Recent overt HE requires driving-safety advice and assessment of falls and caregiver support. Recurrent or severe HE warrants timely transplant evaluation even with a modest MELD score; ACG suggests considering living-donor candidacy when multiple episodes occur with MELD below 15. De-escalation after clinical recompensation is a supervised, stepwise decision with monitoring, not an automatic stop after early cognitive recovery.

check.rationale: The US label indicates reduction in risk of overt HE recurrence in adults at 550 mg twice daily. It does not establish covert HE by a drug response, replace precipitant evaluation or provide systemic sepsis treatment. ACG guidance supports selected acute add-on use, which remains distinct from the labeled prevention indication.

rifaximin-pharmacology-049.question: An adult recovering from recurrent overt HE asks what the US rifaximin indication promises. Which statement is accurate?
choices: It reduces the risk of another overt HE episode.
It establishes HE as the cause of every future episode of confusion.
It reverses cirrhosis and removes the need for liver follow-up.
It replaces systemic antibiotics when sepsis triggers confusion.
rifaximin-pharmacology-049.rationale: The labeled adult HE outcome is reduced overt recurrence risk. It is not a diagnostic test or a cure for liver disease. Low systemic exposure also makes it unsuitable as sole treatment of sepsis; the precipitant and underlying liver disease still require care.

rifaximin-pharmacology-050.question: A 30-day prescription specifies one rifaximin 550 mg tablet twice daily for HE prevention. What quantity supplies the prescribed regimen?
choices: 60 tablets
30 tablets
42 tablets
90 tablets
rifaximin-pharmacology-050.rationale: Two tablets/day × 30 days = 60 tablets, providing 1,100 mg/day. Thirty tablets would supply 15 days; 42 supplies 21 days and 90 supplies 45 days at this frequency. The calculation does not impose a 30-day stopping point on longer-term HE prevention.

rifaximin-pharmacology-051.question: The pivotal HE trial reported 22% breakthrough episodes with rifaximin and 46% with placebo, plus a 58% time-to-event risk reduction. Which interpretation is best?
choices: The reported time-to-event reduction differs from the absolute difference in observed event proportions.
Rifaximin produced a 58-percentage-point absolute reduction.
The trial showed that every patient avoided recurrence.
The result established the same benefit in patients with MELD above 25.
rifaximin-pharmacology-051.rationale: The observed rounded proportions differ by about 24 percentage points; the label reports 58% from its time-to-event comparison. These measures are not interchangeable, and recurrence still occurred. No patients had MELD above 25, so that subgroup was not established by this trial.

rifaximin-pharmacology-052.question: In the label's six-month open-label HE trial, the hazard ratio for rifaximin alone versus rifaximin plus lactulose was 1.98. Which statement is correct?
choices: Monotherapy had a higher breakthrough-HE hazard than combination therapy in that trial.
Monotherapy had a 98-percentage-point lower recurrence rate.
The groups had identical breakthrough-HE outcomes.
The trial proved that no patient can ever use rifaximin without lactulose.
rifaximin-pharmacology-052.rationale: A hazard ratio of 1.98 for monotherapy versus combination indicates approximately 98% higher breakthrough hazard over the studied period; the 95% CI was 1.06 to 3.7. Observed events were 28/113 (25%) versus 15/109 (14%). This open-label comparison supports retaining tolerated lactulose but does not create an absolute prohibition on individualized monotherapy.

rifaximin-pharmacology-053.question: A patient tolerates maintenance lactulose and is starting rifaximin for recurrent overt HE. Which bowel-plan advice is best?
choices: Continue and titrate tolerated lactulose under the care plan rather than stopping it automatically.
Stop lactulose solely because rifaximin has been prescribed.
Replace lactulose with a rifaximin blood-level target.
Increase lactulose until every stool is watery regardless of hydration.
rifaximin-pharmacology-053.rationale: The pivotal placebo-controlled evidence largely included lactulose, and the active-controlled label trial favored combination over rifaximin alone. Retain tolerated lactulose with a goal of about 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Drug levels and excessive watery stools are not prevention targets; significant intolerance warrants reassessment.

rifaximin-pharmacology-054.question: An adult has recurrent overt HE despite adherence to a tolerated lactulose maintenance regimen. Which addition matches ACG guidance and the US prevention dose?
choices: Rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily, with continued trigger and bowel-plan review.
Rifaximin 200 mg orally three times daily for three days as the HE maintenance regimen.
Rifaximin 550 mg orally three times daily for fourteen days as the HE maintenance regimen.
Rifaximin 400 mg orally every eight hours for five days as the labeled HE prevention regimen.
rifaximin-pharmacology-054.rationale: ACG recommends adding rifaximin for recurrent episodes despite lactulose maintenance; the US prevention dose is 550 mg twice daily. The 200 mg three-times-daily three-day regimen is for qualifying travelers' diarrhea and the 550 mg three-times-daily fourteen-day regimen is for IBS-D. The book's older acute off-label schedule is not labeled HE prevention.

rifaximin-pharmacology-055.question: A patient taking lactulose and rifaximin develops eight watery stools daily, weakness and rising sodium. Which response is best?
choices: Reassess excess catharsis, hydration, electrolytes, cognition and lactulose dosing promptly.
Increase lactulose because watery diarrhea proves adequate HE control.
Ignore the fluid loss because rifaximin prevents dehydration-related recurrence.
Adjust rifaximin solely to normalize the ammonia concentration.
rifaximin-pharmacology-055.rationale: Excess lactulose can cause dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities that precipitate HE. The bowel goal is soft stools without harmful fluid loss. Rifaximin does not neutralize these complications and ammonia alone should not drive dosing; persistent or worsening diarrhea also requires consideration of other causes, including C. difficile.

rifaximin-pharmacology-056.question: A team proposes rifaximin added to lactulose during acute overt HE. How should its evidence and indication be described?
choices: ACG 2026 conditionally supports acute add-on use with low-certainty evidence, distinct from the US recurrence label.
The US label specifically establishes rifaximin as stand-alone acute stabilization.
The recommendation means airway and precipitant assessment can be omitted.
The acute setting requires automatic substitution of the IBS-D fourteen-day schedule.
rifaximin-pharmacology-056.rationale: The ACG recommendation for acute add-on rifaximin is conditional with low-certainty evidence. The US HE label addresses reduction in overt recurrence risk. Neither supports omitting airway and trigger care, using rifaximin alone as stabilization or importing the IBS-D regimen.

rifaximin-pharmacology-057.question: A hospitalized patient on rifaximin prevention develops confusion, fever and abdominal discomfort with ascites. Which plan is best?
choices: Evaluate infection, including diagnostic paracentesis, while addressing HE and the identified precipitant.
Assume rifaximin prevents SBP and defer infection assessment.
Wait for ammonia normalization before investigating infection.
Treat suspected sepsis with oral rifaximin alone because it is an antibiotic.
rifaximin-pharmacology-057.rationale: Infection, including SBP, can precipitate HE and independently affect cognition. Hospitalized ascites with suspected infection warrants diagnostic paracentesis and appropriate infection care. Rifaximin prevention does not exclude infection or provide adequate systemic sepsis treatment; ammonia does not determine whether to investigate.

rifaximin-pharmacology-058.question: A patient with prior HE develops confusion and new unilateral arm weakness while taking rifaximin. Which response is safest?
choices: Obtain urgent neurological evaluation and indicated imaging alongside HE assessment.
Attribute the focal deficit to HE without assessing stroke or bleeding.
Wait for a rifaximin concentration before evaluating the deficit.
Omit imaging because guidance discourages it in every patient with cirrhosis.
rifaximin-pharmacology-058.rationale: New focal findings require urgent evaluation for neurological disease. Guidance against routine imaging in typical confusion without new focal deficits does not apply here. Rifaximin levels do not resolve the differential, and HE and a neurological emergency can coexist.

rifaximin-pharmacology-059.question: An obtunded patient with suspected severe HE cannot swallow safely. What takes priority before giving oral rifaximin?
choices: Urgent airway protection and a supervised assessment of treatment route and precipitants.
Forcing the tablet orally to avoid delaying the prevention regimen.
Using a feeding tube as proof that aspiration is impossible.
Waiting for outpatient refill authorization before addressing consciousness.
rifaximin-pharmacology-059.rationale: Severe impaired consciousness requires monitored care and airway assessment. Oral drug administration must account for aspiration risk; a feeding tube alone does not protect the airway. Acute stabilization and treatment of precipitants take priority over routine prevention dispensing.

rifaximin-pharmacology-060.question: A patient on HE prevention becomes confused and an obtained ammonia value is normal. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Reconsider competing causes in addition to HE and use the clinical assessment to guide care.
Exclude HE with certainty solely because ammonia is normal.
Diagnose HE only if a later ammonia value becomes elevated.
Escalate rifaximin solely to reach an ammonia target.
rifaximin-pharmacology-060.rationale: A normal result prompts consideration of other diagnoses rather than automatic exclusion of HE. An elevated result alone would not establish HE either. Clinical examination, time course, precipitants and treatment response guide care; ammonia should not be a stand-alone rifaximin titration target.

rifaximin-pharmacology-061.question: Which follow-up best evaluates whether rifaximin prevention is helping an adult with recurrent overt HE?
choices: Track recurrent episodes, cognition, function, falls, admissions, adherence and bowel safety.
Use routine rifaximin concentrations as the sole effectiveness outcome.
Judge success only by normalization of ammonia despite worsening cognition.
Count dispensed tablets without assessing whether the patient takes them.
rifaximin-pharmacology-061.rationale: Clinical recurrence and function are the meaningful prevention outcomes. Bowel quality, hydration, adherence and access affect the safety and success of the regimen. Neither routine rifaximin levels, ammonia alone nor dispensing counts replace assessment of the patient.

rifaximin-pharmacology-062.question: A caregiver reports that rifaximin will run out before the post-discharge visit because the prescription is unaffordable. Which plan is best?
choices: Resolve access with the care team, arrange supply and a written recurrence plan, and assign follow-up responsibility.
Wait for another admission before addressing the medication gap.
Replace the prescription with the travelers' diarrhea three-day schedule without review.
Stop all HE prevention once discharge cognition is normal.
rifaximin-pharmacology-062.rationale: An effective plan requires accessible medicines, caregiver instructions and a clear monitoring owner. Address a foreseeable lapse before it occurs; the schedule remains indication-specific. Recovery at discharge does not automatically end recurrence prevention.

rifaximin-pharmacology-063.question: An outpatient with recurrent HE, muscle loss and MELD below 15 asks whether severe protein restriction will replace rifaximin and liver follow-up. Which response is best?
choices: Maintain adequate individualized protein intake and arrange HE and transplant assessment rather than substituting protein restriction.
Use severe protein restriction as the primary recurrence-prevention treatment.
Defer transplant evaluation solely because MELD is below 15.
Stop rifaximin permanently whenever confusion improves for one day.
rifaximin-pharmacology-063.rationale: ACG recommends 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein in outpatients with HE and advises against routine protein restriction. Recurrent HE warrants liver and transplant assessment; ACG suggests considering living-donor candidacy with multiple episodes despite MELD below 15. Nutrition and temporary cognitive recovery do not independently authorize stopping prevention.

rifaximin-pharmacology-064.question: A patient with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis needs rifaximin prevention and takes cyclosporine. Which safety assessment is correct?
choices: Severe hepatic impairment and P-gp inhibition can increase exposure and require careful review and caution.
Minimal usual absorption makes the combination free of interaction risk.
Child-Pugh C impairment is an absolute labeled contraindication equivalent to rifamycin allergy.
The label requires an automatic unvalidated dose reduction based solely on Child-Pugh class.
rifaximin-pharmacology-064.rationale: The label cautions in severe hepatic impairment and with P-gp inhibitors such as cyclosporine, which may further increase systemic exposure. It recommends no routine hepatic dose adjustment because of local action. Severe impairment is a caution, while rifaximin/rifamycin/product hypersensitivity is a contraindication; patient-specific review is still needed.

rifaximin-pharmacology-160.rationale: Adult overt HE recurrence prevention uses 550 mg twice daily. The 200 mg three-times-daily three-day regimen is for qualifying travelers' diarrhea, and 550 mg three times daily for fourteen days is the IBS-D regimen. A 400 mg three-times-daily twenty-day course belongs to a distinct off-label recurrent-CDI sequence. Continue the individualized lactulose, precipitant and follow-up plan; the HE label does not specify a fixed short course.

Vegetable or dairy protein can support tolerance without becoming a reason to underfeed. BCAA supplementation can be considered when food alone cannot meet protein needs. Zinc is an adjunct for documented low zinc with persistent symptoms despite lactulose and rifaximin, not a universal substitute for either medicine.
wholeBodies.review: Complete paragraph compared again with the indicated source sections, including exact indication, population, dose, evidence certainty, monitoring and uncertainty qualifiers.

wholeBodies.heading: Reassess persistent disease and procedure-related risk
wholeBodies.body: If mental status does not recover after 48 to 72 hours of adequate therapy and precipitant reversal, reassess missed infection, drugs, metabolic or neurological disease and portosystemic shunts. Deterioration requires immediate care rather than waiting for that interval. Refractory HE may warrant specialist shunt assessment. Separately, ACG 2026 recommends starting rifaximin 14 days before elective TIPS and continuing for at least six months in decompensated cirrhosis, with or without previous overt HE. This is procedure-specific guidance beyond the labeled recurrence indication; it is not a reason to delay an emergency procedure.
wholeBodies.review: Complete paragraph compared again with the indicated source sections, including exact indication, population, dose, evidence certainty, monitoring and uncertainty qualifiers.

wholeBodies.heading: Make prevention executable
wholeBodies.body: Assign a clinician to follow recurrence, tolerance and liver progression. Provide patients and caregivers a written bowel plan, reliable medication supply and instructions for worsening confusion, bleeding, fever, profuse diarrhea or inability to take medicines. Address affordability and refill interruptions before discharge. Recent overt HE requires driving-safety advice and assessment of falls and caregiver support. Recurrent or severe HE warrants timely transplant evaluation even with a modest MELD score; ACG suggests considering living-donor candidacy when multiple episodes occur with MELD below 15. De-escalation after clinical recompensation is a supervised, stepwise decision with monitoring, not an automatic stop after early cognitive recovery.

object.question: What is rifaximin's labeled hepatic encephalopathy role?
choices: Reducing recurrent overt episodes in adults
Diagnosing covert HE
Replacing all precipitant evaluation
Treating systemic sepsis
object.rationale: The US label indicates reduction in risk of overt HE recurrence in adults at 550 mg twice daily. It does not establish covert HE by a drug response, replace precipitant evaluation or provide systemic sepsis treatment. ACG guidance supports selected acute add-on use, which remains distinct from the labeled prevention indication.

wholeCheck.singleBestAnswerReview: The US label indicates reduction in risk of overt HE recurrence in adults at 550 mg twice daily. It does not establish covert HE by a drug response, replace precipitant evaluation or provide systemic sepsis treatment. ACG guidance supports selected acute add-on use, which remains distinct from the labeled prevention indication.

figure.title: Rifaximin works inside a broader hepatic encephalopathy plan
figure.review: All 18 caption/node text elements reviewed as an original clinical-care summary. Does not promise recovery or imply rifaximin alone stabilizes acute disease.

wholeObject.question: An adult recovering from recurrent overt HE asks what the US rifaximin indication promises. Which statement is accurate?
choices: It reduces the risk of another overt HE episode.
It establishes HE as the cause of every future episode of confusion.
It reverses cirrhosis and removes the need for liver follow-up.
It replaces systemic antibiotics when sepsis triggers confusion.
wholeObject.rationale: The labeled adult HE outcome is reduced overt recurrence risk. It is not a diagnostic test or a cure for liver disease. Low systemic exposure also makes it unsuitable as sole treatment of sepsis; the precipitant and underlying liver disease still require care.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The labeled adult HE outcome is reduced overt recurrence risk. It is not a diagnostic test or a cure for liver disease. Low systemic exposure also makes it unsuitable as sole treatment of sepsis; the precipitant and underlying liver disease still require care.

wholeObject.question: A 30-day prescription specifies one rifaximin 550 mg tablet twice daily for HE prevention. What quantity supplies the prescribed regimen?
choices: 60 tablets
30 tablets
42 tablets
90 tablets
wholeObject.rationale: Two tablets/day × 30 days = 60 tablets, providing 1,100 mg/day. Thirty tablets would supply 15 days; 42 supplies 21 days and 90 supplies 45 days at this frequency. The calculation does not impose a 30-day stopping point on longer-term HE prevention.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Two tablets/day × 30 days = 60 tablets, providing 1,100 mg/day. Thirty tablets would supply 15 days; 42 supplies 21 days and 90 supplies 45 days at this frequency. The calculation does not impose a 30-day stopping point on longer-term HE prevention.

wholeObject.question: The pivotal HE trial reported 22% breakthrough episodes with rifaximin and 46% with placebo, plus a 58% time-to-event risk reduction. Which interpretation is best?
choices: The reported time-to-event reduction differs from the absolute difference in observed event proportions.
Rifaximin produced a 58-percentage-point absolute reduction.
The trial showed that every patient avoided recurrence.
The result established the same benefit in patients with MELD above 25.
wholeObject.rationale: The observed rounded proportions differ by about 24 percentage points; the label reports 58% from its time-to-event comparison. These measures are not interchangeable, and recurrence still occurred. No patients had MELD above 25, so that subgroup was not established by this trial.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The observed rounded proportions differ by about 24 percentage points; the label reports 58% from its time-to-event comparison. These measures are not interchangeable, and recurrence still occurred. No patients had MELD above 25, so that subgroup was not established by this trial.

wholeObject.question: In the label's six-month open-label HE trial, the hazard ratio for rifaximin alone versus rifaximin plus lactulose was 1.98. Which statement is correct?
choices: Monotherapy had a higher breakthrough-HE hazard than combination therapy in that trial.
Monotherapy had a 98-percentage-point lower recurrence rate.
The groups had identical breakthrough-HE outcomes.
The trial proved that no patient can ever use rifaximin without lactulose.
wholeObject.rationale: A hazard ratio of 1.98 for monotherapy versus combination indicates approximately 98% higher breakthrough hazard over the studied period; the 95% CI was 1.06 to 3.7. Observed events were 28/113 (25%) versus 15/109 (14%). This open-label comparison supports retaining tolerated lactulose but does not create an absolute prohibition on individualized monotherapy.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: A hazard ratio of 1.98 for monotherapy versus combination indicates approximately 98% higher breakthrough hazard over the studied period; the 95% CI was 1.06 to 3.7. Observed events were 28/113 (25%) versus 15/109 (14%). This open-label comparison supports retaining tolerated lactulose but does not create an absolute prohibition on individualized monotherapy.

wholeObject.question: A patient tolerates maintenance lactulose and is starting rifaximin for recurrent overt HE. Which bowel-plan advice is best?
choices: Continue and titrate tolerated lactulose under the care plan rather than stopping it automatically.
Stop lactulose solely because rifaximin has been prescribed.
Replace lactulose with a rifaximin blood-level target.
Increase lactulose until every stool is watery regardless of hydration.
wholeObject.rationale: The pivotal placebo-controlled evidence largely included lactulose, and the active-controlled label trial favored combination over rifaximin alone. Retain tolerated lactulose with a goal of about 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Drug levels and excessive watery stools are not prevention targets; significant intolerance warrants reassessment.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The pivotal placebo-controlled evidence largely included lactulose, and the active-controlled label trial favored combination over rifaximin alone. Retain tolerated lactulose with a goal of about 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Drug levels and excessive watery stools are not prevention targets; significant intolerance warrants reassessment.

wholeObject.question: An adult has recurrent overt HE despite adherence to a tolerated lactulose maintenance regimen. Which addition matches ACG guidance and the US prevention dose?
choices: Rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily, with continued trigger and bowel-plan review.
Rifaximin 200 mg orally three times daily for three days as the HE maintenance regimen.
Rifaximin 550 mg orally three times daily for fourteen days as the HE maintenance regimen.
Rifaximin 400 mg orally every eight hours for five days as the labeled HE prevention regimen.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG recommends adding rifaximin for recurrent episodes despite lactulose maintenance; the US prevention dose is 550 mg twice daily. The 200 mg three-times-daily three-day regimen is for qualifying travelers' diarrhea and the 550 mg three-times-daily fourteen-day regimen is for IBS-D. The book's older acute off-label schedule is not labeled HE prevention.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG recommends adding rifaximin for recurrent episodes despite lactulose maintenance; the US prevention dose is 550 mg twice daily. The 200 mg three-times-daily three-day regimen is for qualifying travelers' diarrhea and the 550 mg three-times-daily fourteen-day regimen is for IBS-D. The book's older acute off-label schedule is not labeled HE prevention.

wholeObject.question: A patient taking lactulose and rifaximin develops eight watery stools daily, weakness and rising sodium. Which response is best?
choices: Reassess excess catharsis, hydration, electrolytes, cognition and lactulose dosing promptly.
Increase lactulose because watery diarrhea proves adequate HE control.
Ignore the fluid loss because rifaximin prevents dehydration-related recurrence.
Adjust rifaximin solely to normalize the ammonia concentration.
wholeObject.rationale: Excess lactulose can cause dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities that precipitate HE. The bowel goal is soft stools without harmful fluid loss. Rifaximin does not neutralize these complications and ammonia alone should not drive dosing; persistent or worsening diarrhea also requires consideration of other causes, including C. difficile.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Excess lactulose can cause dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities that precipitate HE. The bowel goal is soft stools without harmful fluid loss. Rifaximin does not neutralize these complications and ammonia alone should not drive dosing; persistent or worsening diarrhea also requires consideration of other causes, including C. difficile.

wholeObject.question: A team proposes rifaximin added to lactulose during acute overt HE. How should its evidence and indication be described?
choices: ACG 2026 conditionally supports acute add-on use with low-certainty evidence, distinct from the US recurrence label.
The US label specifically establishes rifaximin as stand-alone acute stabilization.
The recommendation means airway and precipitant assessment can be omitted.
The acute setting requires automatic substitution of the IBS-D fourteen-day schedule.
wholeObject.rationale: The ACG recommendation for acute add-on rifaximin is conditional with low-certainty evidence. The US HE label addresses reduction in overt recurrence risk. Neither supports omitting airway and trigger care, using rifaximin alone as stabilization or importing the IBS-D regimen.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The ACG recommendation for acute add-on rifaximin is conditional with low-certainty evidence. The US HE label addresses reduction in overt recurrence risk. Neither supports omitting airway and trigger care, using rifaximin alone as stabilization or importing the IBS-D regimen.

wholeObject.question: A hospitalized patient on rifaximin prevention develops confusion, fever and abdominal discomfort with ascites. Which plan is best?
choices: Evaluate infection, including diagnostic paracentesis, while addressing HE and the identified precipitant.
Assume rifaximin prevents SBP and defer infection assessment.
Wait for ammonia normalization before investigating infection.
Treat suspected sepsis with oral rifaximin alone because it is an antibiotic.
wholeObject.rationale: Infection, including SBP, can precipitate HE and independently affect cognition. Hospitalized ascites with suspected infection warrants diagnostic paracentesis and appropriate infection care. Rifaximin prevention does not exclude infection or provide adequate systemic sepsis treatment; ammonia does not determine whether to investigate.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Infection, including SBP, can precipitate HE and independently affect cognition. Hospitalized ascites with suspected infection warrants diagnostic paracentesis and appropriate infection care. Rifaximin prevention does not exclude infection or provide adequate systemic sepsis treatment; ammonia does not determine whether to investigate.

wholeObject.question: A patient with prior HE develops confusion and new unilateral arm weakness while taking rifaximin. Which response is safest?
choices: Obtain urgent neurological evaluation and indicated imaging alongside HE assessment.
Attribute the focal deficit to HE without assessing stroke or bleeding.
Wait for a rifaximin concentration before evaluating the deficit.
Omit imaging because guidance discourages it in every patient with cirrhosis.
wholeObject.rationale: New focal findings require urgent evaluation for neurological disease. Guidance against routine imaging in typical confusion without new focal deficits does not apply here. Rifaximin levels do not resolve the differential, and HE and a neurological emergency can coexist.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: New focal findings require urgent evaluation for neurological disease. Guidance against routine imaging in typical confusion without new focal deficits does not apply here. Rifaximin levels do not resolve the differential, and HE and a neurological emergency can coexist.

wholeObject.question: An obtunded patient with suspected severe HE cannot swallow safely. What takes priority before giving oral rifaximin?
choices: Urgent airway protection and a supervised assessment of treatment route and precipitants.
Forcing the tablet orally to avoid delaying the prevention regimen.
Using a feeding tube as proof that aspiration is impossible.
Waiting for outpatient refill authorization before addressing consciousness.
wholeObject.rationale: Severe impaired consciousness requires monitored care and airway assessment. Oral drug administration must account for aspiration risk; a feeding tube alone does not protect the airway. Acute stabilization and treatment of precipitants take priority over routine prevention dispensing.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Severe impaired consciousness requires monitored care and airway assessment. Oral drug administration must account for aspiration risk; a feeding tube alone does not protect the airway. Acute stabilization and treatment of precipitants take priority over routine prevention dispensing.

wholeObject.question: A patient on HE prevention becomes confused and an obtained ammonia value is normal. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Reconsider competing causes in addition to HE and use the clinical assessment to guide care.
Exclude HE with certainty solely because ammonia is normal.
Diagnose HE only if a later ammonia value becomes elevated.
Escalate rifaximin solely to reach an ammonia target.
wholeObject.rationale: A normal result prompts consideration of other diagnoses rather than automatic exclusion of HE. An elevated result alone would not establish HE either. Clinical examination, time course, precipitants and treatment response guide care; ammonia should not be a stand-alone rifaximin titration target.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: A normal result prompts consideration of other diagnoses rather than automatic exclusion of HE. An elevated result alone would not establish HE either. Clinical examination, time course, precipitants and treatment response guide care; ammonia should not be a stand-alone rifaximin titration target.

wholeObject.question: Which follow-up best evaluates whether rifaximin prevention is helping an adult with recurrent overt HE?
choices: Track recurrent episodes, cognition, function, falls, admissions, adherence and bowel safety.
Use routine rifaximin concentrations as the sole effectiveness outcome.
Judge success only by normalization of ammonia despite worsening cognition.
Count dispensed tablets without assessing whether the patient takes them.
wholeObject.rationale: Clinical recurrence and function are the meaningful prevention outcomes. Bowel quality, hydration, adherence and access affect the safety and success of the regimen. Neither routine rifaximin levels, ammonia alone nor dispensing counts replace assessment of the patient.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Clinical recurrence and function are the meaningful prevention outcomes. Bowel quality, hydration, adherence and access affect the safety and success of the regimen. Neither routine rifaximin levels, ammonia alone nor dispensing counts replace assessment of the patient.

wholeObject.question: A caregiver reports that rifaximin will run out before the post-discharge visit because the prescription is unaffordable. Which plan is best?
choices: Resolve access with the care team, arrange supply and a written recurrence plan, and assign follow-up responsibility.
Wait for another admission before addressing the medication gap.
Replace the prescription with the travelers' diarrhea three-day schedule without review.
Stop all HE prevention once discharge cognition is normal.
wholeObject.rationale: An effective plan requires accessible medicines, caregiver instructions and a clear monitoring owner. Address a foreseeable lapse before it occurs; the schedule remains indication-specific. Recovery at discharge does not automatically end recurrence prevention.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: An effective plan requires accessible medicines, caregiver instructions and a clear monitoring owner. Address a foreseeable lapse before it occurs; the schedule remains indication-specific. Recovery at discharge does not automatically end recurrence prevention.

wholeObject.question: An outpatient with recurrent HE, muscle loss and MELD below 15 asks whether severe protein restriction will replace rifaximin and liver follow-up. Which response is best?
choices: Maintain adequate individualized protein intake and arrange HE and transplant assessment rather than substituting protein restriction.
Use severe protein restriction as the primary recurrence-prevention treatment.
Defer transplant evaluation solely because MELD is below 15.
Stop rifaximin permanently whenever confusion improves for one day.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG recommends 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein in outpatients with HE and advises against routine protein restriction. Recurrent HE warrants liver and transplant assessment; ACG suggests considering living-donor candidacy with multiple episodes despite MELD below 15. Nutrition and temporary cognitive recovery do not independently authorize stopping prevention.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG recommends 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day protein in outpatients with HE and advises against routine protein restriction. Recurrent HE warrants liver and transplant assessment; ACG suggests considering living-donor candidacy with multiple episodes despite MELD below 15. Nutrition and temporary cognitive recovery do not independently authorize stopping prevention.

wholeObject.question: A patient with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis needs rifaximin prevention and takes cyclosporine. Which safety assessment is correct?
choices: Severe hepatic impairment and P-gp inhibition can increase exposure and require careful review and caution.
Minimal usual absorption makes the combination free of interaction risk.
Child-Pugh C impairment is an absolute labeled contraindication equivalent to rifamycin allergy.
The label requires an automatic unvalidated dose reduction based solely on Child-Pugh class.
wholeObject.rationale: The label cautions in severe hepatic impairment and with P-gp inhibitors such as cyclosporine, which may further increase systemic exposure. It recommends no routine hepatic dose adjustment because of local action. Severe impairment is a caution, while rifaximin/rifamycin/product hypersensitivity is a contraindication; patient-specific review is still needed.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: The label cautions in severe hepatic impairment and with P-gp inhibitors such as cyclosporine, which may further increase systemic exposure. It recommends no routine hepatic dose adjustment because of local action. Severe impairment is a caution, while rifaximin/rifamycin/product hypersensitivity is a contraindication; patient-specific review is still needed.

wholeObject.question: A patient with recurrent overt HE takes lactulose but has repeated admissions. Which rifaximin regimen matches the label?
choices: 550 mg twice daily
200 mg three times daily for 3 days
550 mg three times daily for 14 days
400 mg three times daily for 20 days
wholeObject.rationale: Adult overt HE recurrence prevention uses 550 mg twice daily. The 200 mg three-times-daily three-day regimen is for qualifying travelers' diarrhea, and 550 mg three times daily for fourteen days is the IBS-D regimen. A 400 mg three-times-daily twenty-day course belongs to a distinct off-label recurrent-CDI sequence. Continue the individualized lactulose, precipitant and follow-up plan; the HE label does not specify a fixed short course.

wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Adult overt HE recurrence prevention uses 550 mg twice daily. The 200 mg three-times-daily three-day regimen is for qualifying travelers' diarrhea, and 550 mg three times daily for fourteen days is the IBS-D regimen. A 400 mg three-times-daily twenty-day course belongs to a distinct off-label recurrent-CDI sequence. Continue the individualized lactulose, precipitant and follow-up plan; the HE label does not specify a fixed short course.

discrepancies.issue: Sixteen generated HE prompts have multiple true choices or multiple harmful choices.
discrepancies.resolution: Replace them with distinct single-best-answer clinical, calculation and evidence-interpretation cases. Preserve all IDs, keys, lesson anchors, field presence and ordering. Retain useful dose case 160 and explain all its choices.

discrepancies.issue: The four-body lesson omits the active-controlled monotherapy versus combination trial in the current label.
discrepancies.resolution: Teach both trials, concomitant lactulose, denominators, six-month populations, recurrence/hospitalization endpoints and limits. Do not equate time-to-event effects with absolute percentage-point changes.

discrepancies.issue: The label Trial 2 Figure 3 vertical-axis wording refers to HE-related hospitalization while its title and primary endpoint specify breakthrough HE.
discrepancies.resolution: Use the explicit primary-endpoint definition, results and title for teaching; retain this source discrepancy and do not reproduce that axis as a claim. No official-source alteration performed.

discrepancies.issue: Book acute rifaximin 400 mg every eight hours for five to ten days can be confused with labeled recurrence prevention.
discrepancies.resolution: Separate historical off-label acute dosing, current conditional low-certainty acute add-on guidance and labeled 550 mg twice-daily prevention.

discrepancies.issue: Book ammonia monitoring and protein restriction wording can be carried into current prevention teaching.
discrepancies.resolution: Use current clinical assessment and bowel/hydration monitoring, normal-ammonia differential reassessment, adequate outpatient protein and muscle care; no ammonia-only titration or routine protein restriction.

discrepancies.issue: Low absorption can be misread as no severe-hepatic or interaction risk.
discrepancies.resolution: Retain label exposure data, no routine hepatic dose adjustment plus Child-Pugh C caution, P-gp exposure and warfarin monitoring, allergy/CDI/skin and muscle safety.

discrepancies.issue: Module sourceNotes.reviewed implies the complete parent was already reconciled despite its unreviewed ledger.
discrepancies.resolution: Replace the unsupported completed-review wording with a neutral reference description. The ledger certifies only this complete HE lesson and 17 anchored questions; other nine lessons and 147 questions remain pending.
